articles.title: The Sinking City 2 Is a Praiseworthy Blend of Lovecraft and Resident Evil
articles.summary: The Sinking City 2 feels inescapably like off-brand Resident Evil, but it's a praiseworthy imitation of its main inspirations wrapped in the Cthulhu mythos.
articles.body:
It was impossible for me to play The Sinking City 2 for more than 15 minutes without coming to the obvious realization that this is Resident Evil in a fedora. That might sound dismissive, but I really enjoy the recent Resident Evil games, so comparing Frogwares' Lovecraftian survival horror sequel to some of the best of them – which feels especially similar to 2019's Resident Evil 2 remake – is much more of a compliment than a put-down. What sets it apart begins with its unique, rich, 1920s New England setting flush with loving detail that instills a strong sense of personality over the top of the mechanics it so clearly imitates.

You play as Calvin Rafferty, a likeable occultist waking up to an apocalyptic flood set to wipe out the entire city of Arkham, Massachusetts in 1929. He's definitely a little bit of a pulp fiction stock character: hard-chinned, two-fisted, and foolishly brave. But there are layers to him that rise to the surface here and there. Similar to the Resident Evil comparison, likening him to the classic heroes of the genre is not really an insult.

The intriguing cosmic horror plot revolves around a half-remembered expedition to Lovecraft's surreal Dreamlands that left Calvin's partner and paramour, Faye, in a comatose state. This creates immediate emotional stakes and momentum from the very start, which carried me through the somewhat slow first half of the first chapter. I don't want to spoil too many surprises, but The Sinking City 2 manages to be a bit of a who's who of the Cthulhu mythos. Some of its eldritch guest characters are much more hinted at than portrayed in all their terrible glory, but Arkham-heads will find lots of little nods to make them cackle with otherworldly glee.

The unfolding story includes some effective emotional beats and a few neat twists that kept me guessing about some characters' motivations, but overall remains pretty easy to follow given the high concept subject matter. This isn't the kind of tale where you're going to have to look up a YouTube video to explain the ending afterwards, and I appreciated that. But it also doesn't back down from engaging with some of the heavier metaphysical aspects of Lovecraft, effectively selling the idea that you're up against beings beyond human comprehension. And it also does a decent job of sidestepping some of the ones that haven't aged particularly well.

The centerpiece is the town of Arkham itself, which presents a gorgeously damp and decrepit backdrop for exploration and combat. Excellent texture work and sound design come together to create an atmosphere that made my skin feel clammy even in the dry heat of a Colorado summer. The density of little details crammed into every corner of every area is truly inspiring. Every dilapidated hotel room or terrifying hospital ward feels both lived-in and ravaged by the ongoing disaster. The cutscenes and facial animations aren't always to the same level of quality, but pretty strong voice acting across the board helps carry them past their production limitations.

Each chapter takes you to a new locale in Arkham, and each feels distinct in both vibes and layout. You start out in the flooded city streets, navigating by boat to various ruins and culminating in a creepy, haunted hotel. Chapter 2, which I found to be the scariest, is set in an abandoned hospital that features its own version of the unkillable stalker in the spirit of Mr. X and Nemesis. And Chapter 3 takes you to the Arkham Fish Market, which goes about exactly how you'd expect if you're familiar with the works of Lovecraft. That is to say, very poorly for our boy Calvin in some unpleasantly fish-themed ways. This progression keeps things fresh while maintaining a cohesive aesthetic.

As I mentioned earlier, when it comes to the mechanics, this is an unapologetic tribute to modern, over-the-shoulder Resident Evil. Calvin can amass a small arsenal of guns, but there are never enough bullets to kill everything, leading to tense scrounging through drawers for every last round. Melee is an option, but not a very effective one. Mixing it up with even your basic zombie-like enemies is almost a guarantee of taking some licks yourself, so close quarters combat became a conscious choice to expend my healing items instead of my ammo. Calvin is not as vulnerable as Resident Evil Requiem's Grace, but he's certainly not a Leon S. Kennedy-level action hero, maintaining a good balance between competent and fragile.

The controls are very similar. The inventory system is very similar. The basic enemies are very similar. There are puzzles where you have to find three things to stick into a door to make it open. You can pick up herbs and craft them into healing items. It even has a system of achievements that unlock powerful perks in New Game+ almost identical to the newer Resident Evil games. Again, I'm not complaining. It's not like I'm sick of the modern Resident Evil formula if it's executed well, and Frogwares did a commendable job, so this feels like a free extra course while we wait for Capcom's next big dish.

One exception to the scarce ammo rule is that certain boss fights or big arena battles have infinitely respawning loot pick-ups (explained by an in-game note that lampshades their bizarre physical properties) to keep you from getting softlocked if your magazines run dry. This felt like a little bit of a cop-out that undermines its difficulty – these segments were some of my least favorite anyway, but hey, you know what else is very Resident Evil? Having boss fights that aren't very good.

All that said, The Sinking City 2 isn't just about Frogwares being a Capcom cover band. One way it sets itself apart is with a perk system that lets you unlock and equip powerful runes that do things like increase your damage when your flashlight is off, rewarding you for being able to hit enemies you can't even see. They come in four tiers of increasing power, and you can't really unlock the strongest ones on a single playthrough, creating a compelling incentive to charge headlong into horror all over again.

The other novel bit is the ability to find written clues around every area that can be organized and connected with red strands like your very own wacky conspiracy board. Each belongs to a group, and correctly connecting each group gives you some progression points. Some give hints on plot-critical objectives, while others point to potent, optional treasures. The rewards feel worthwhile, though some require a little bit of backtracking, even if the puzzles themselves aren't exactly brain-busters.

You can set the difficulty of these puzzles independently of the combat difficulty, which is neat, but all the harder option really does is remove highlighted text and icons that tell you which clues belong together. I didn't find it particularly difficult to figure out which hints were related and put together the information in them myself even without those hints, so it felt like increasing the difficulty from Very Easy to Easy. There is one pretty tough optional puzzle that required me to really use my brain later on, but I did end up yearning for more difficult detective work.

Also, there is no sanity mechanic, which seems a little odd for a Cthulhu game. There are some strange moments of reality-bending theatrics, but I was never made to doubt if the things my character was experiencing were even real. And that's a bit of a letdown.

articles.title: These Three 1970s Hammer Horror Movies, Out Now in a Beautiful New 4K Set, Are Must-Watch Titles for Any Fan
articles.summary: Sangster Directs Hammer review: Severin Films focuses on the considerable contribution of writer/director Jimmy Sangster (and actor Ralph Bates) to Hammer horror film history.
articles.body:
In the early ’70s, UK-based Hammer Films was winding down after defining a creative and colorful era of horror with lavishly produced films featuring lovely ladies, lethal living dead, and copious amounts of red, red blood. But even though their greatest years were behind them, the company that made Christopher Lee and Peter Cushing genre icons still had a few devilish delights to offer audiences before they reached the end of that dirt road in their runaway carriage (either 1976 for their last horror film, To the Devil a Daughter, or 1979, when they released their actual last film, Hitchcock remake The Lady Vanishes). One of the men most responsible for writing many of the movies that shaped Hammer’s style, Jimmy Sangster, even got a chance to direct during that final decade of Hammer’s classic output, and although the three films he helmed (two of which he also co-wrote, while the other — Lust for a Vampire — was scripted by Danger: Diabolik and Barbarella ’s Tudor Gates) are not generally regarded as among the best the studio produced, they each have charms all their own and deserve reappraisal.

Now Severin Films is giving us that opportunity with their first-ever release of Hammer titles — Sangster Directs Hammer is an impressive set that brings The Horror of Frankenstein (1970), Lust for a Vampire (1971), and Fear in the Night (1972) to the US in 4K UHD for the first time, all wrapped up in a gorgeously gory green box. As usual for Severin, these movies have never looked this vibrant. Hammer was always well known for its lurid palette and stunning visuals, but now they practically leap off the screen. Fortunately, Severin also knows that preserving the true film experience is important, so grain is not absent but a wonderful texture layer along with everything else. One minor tweak: The box would perhaps be better named Sangster Directs Hammer’s Ralph Bates, because that actor — who forged a productive creative partnership and lasting friendship with the director — appears in all three films, and the story of their collaboration is the spine running through the patchwork body of material presented here. As for the extraordinary extras curated and collected to accompany the films — including a 312-page book! — there couldn’t be a better sign of the love and respect that everyone involved has for these movies and the creative team that made them.

Sangster was an endearingly self-deprecating man who, in his autobiography Do You Want It Good or Tuesday, titled the chapter on these three films “They Would Have Been Better Directed by Terry Fisher” (referring to the legendary Hammer director who helmed multiple entries in their Frankenstein and Dracula series starting with the first installments in 1957 and 1958 respectively). We’ll never know if that would actually be true, but that doesn’t mean these movies are the failures Sangster and others believed. Most folks apparently shuffle these to the bottom of their lists pretty quickly; the fact that Severin was only able to produce this box because no one else wanted to license these titles is baffling to me, but a boon for us and them. And no, I’m not saying these are classics on par with the films that launched Hammer’s legend, but they’re solid productions with something to offer both Hammer aficionados and casual fans alike. Let’s take a closer look…

Of the many tactics Hammer employed to distinguish their cinematic monsters from the unforgettable 1930s-1940s Universal incarnations that preceded them, one of the cleverest and most inventive was to follow the creator rather than the creature when making their series of Frankenstein films. And I know it’s blasphemy to many Hammer fans (appropriately enough) but this comedic remake of Hammer’s first Frankenstein foray (1957’s The Curse of Frankenstein) and the next-to-last installment in the seven-film Hammer Frankenstein series — with Ralph Bates replacing Peter Cushing as Victor — is my favorite of that entire run. While Cushing plays an utter sociopath or a more genial amoral Victor well (there are two timelines in the series; it’s complicated), Bates perfectly blends the sociopathy with a glib devil-may-care charm that makes him delightfully magnetic. Hammer was trying to make Bates a thing, positioning him as Frankenstein, Dracula (plans for that went awry when Christopher Lee came back instead, relegating Bates to a smaller role in 1970's Taste the Blood of Dracula), and Dr. Jekyll (in 1971's Dr. Jekyll and Sister Hyde). While things didn’t quite pan out, what we have is wonderful for all of us who value what Bates brought to the slab.

The film is ahead of its time with its black humor and gleeful lewdness; it feels like partial inspiration for the Re-Animator movies, and its lascivious tone resembles what people often thought all Hammer movies were like but weren’t . The sexual dynamics are interesting too, as Victor’s friend, Stephan (Stephen Turner), eagerly becomes his cook and wants very much to be part of Victor’s life, while the movie makes clear that a man working in the kitchen seems unusual to everyone. They also joke about Victor not being interested in men...or is he? He shows zero interest in Elizabeth (Hammer regular Veronica Carlson) even when she virtually proposes to him, and although he carries on with housekeeper Alys (the superb Kate O’Mara), that could be more about continuing a power dynamic established by his father rather than personal desire.

In a cute twist on Frankenstein tropes, Victor keeps track of creature assembly via a build-by-numbers approach. His friend Wilhelm (Graham James) even hits the nail on the flattop by speaking a version of the clichéd line: “You’re tampering with forces we don’t fully understand!” As for the creature itself, David Prowse (yes, Darth Vader) is a mute, hairless Karloffian monster with a creepy smugness that suggests he’s far smarter than his predecessors. He’s no tragic figure either; this creature’s a violent bastard . As the bodies mount up, Victor is willing to let those around him suffer if it means protecting his creation; the apple didn’t reanimate far from the tree.

The only disappointment is an abrupt ending that leaves you wanting Bates-led sequels, but it wasn’t to be; when Hammer tried one more time to draw on Shelley’s creation for movie material, they brought Cushing back. But we have this one, and it’s a twisted delight.

After mining Stoker for over a decade, Hammer turned to Sheridan Le Fanu’s sapphic classic novel, Carmilla, for inspiration, resulting in a trio of films focusing on a female vampire first played by Ingrid Pitt in 1970’s lush and top-heavy saucy romp, The Vampire Lovers. Lust for a Vampire is the second installment in what would later be labeled “The Karnstein Trilogy,” and it featured several missteps, not least replacing Pitt as Mircalla/Carmilla with Yutte Stensgaard. Yutte’s no Ingrid, but she’s also not as bad as some think. She does a damn good job of conveying that underlying air of menace and calculation that makes Carmilla a great villain; she just isn’t quite as good or as stylish as Pitt was.

Also carrying over from the first Karnstein film is the character of the “Man in Black,” a sort of/not really Dracula played this time by Mike Raven (there are odd cutaway insert shots of Christopher Lee’s eyes to muddy the waters). Unlike the mute grinning fool from the first movie played by John Forbes-Robertson, this one — now more specifically Count Karnstein — speaks with the dubbed voice of Valentine Dyall, but his role is still murky. He’s partnered with the Countess (Barbara Jefford), but more intriguing than the Man in Black’s part in this tale is the behind-the-scenes goss on Raven himself; for that, go to the extras and the book.

Ralph Bates (who replaced Cushing in this particular role) famously threw this movie under the bus, but damn if he doesn’t give his performance as the creepy teacher at a girls' school 110%; he’s one of the highlights of the movie. Our hero, new teacher Richard LeStrange (Michael Johnson), is based on Carmilla author Le Fanu, and his romance with Carmilla provides Hammer with a chance to immediately dial down the lesbian themes from the first film by focusing Carmilla’s attention primarily on the dashing scholar. Fans also remember (and correctly malign) this one for the insufferable song “Strange Love” that plays not once but twice in a row (the second time with a color-washed montage of previous scenes!) to provide padding as the story isn’t substantial enough for feature length.

The resurrection sequence is pretty spectacular, although you don’t see as much of Yutte as you do in the associated publicity stills (Severin helpfully puts one of those on the cover of the book). There are also nice stylistic touches like mesmerized girls approaching the camera in close-up so that the viewer shares Carmilla’s POV, and the strange mythology of the Karnstein vampires adding the odd twist that simply turning a cross upside down “deactivates” its effects. There are other tropes galore, like an old-school torch-bearing crowd and characters professing deep and abiding love for one another after knowing each other for about an hour. OK, so it’s not Hammer’s finest moment, or even the best of the Karnstein films, but it has its charms as all of them do, and it’s good to have it as part of this set.

Hammer did more than just produce gothic period-set horrors, and that included a series of psychological thrillers often featuring a character fighting for their sanity and their very life. Sangster wrote several of these “Mini-Hitchcocks”; although they were so named because of the debt they owed to the Master of Suspense, the real inspiration for Sangster was Henri-Georges Clouzot’s Les Diaboliques (1955). In fact, he drew on that source more than once, and when it came time not just to write but direct one himself, he reworked his script from an earlier production — 1961’s Scream of Fear — that leaned heavily on its Diabolique origins. Fear in the Night was the result, and despite its present-day setting, it still manages to be pretty gothic with an unsettling psychosexual edge.

Also betraying a possible influence from Italian giallos, especially with the stalker’s black gloved hands, and sharing elements with many of the thrillers and slashers that came before and after it, Fear takes us to a secluded country school where a mentally fragile young newlywed (Judy Geeson of To Sir, with Love) moves with her husband teacher (Ralph Bates of course) into a cottage on the grounds. The headmaster (Peter Cushing) and his wife (Joan Collins) are strangely fascinated with Geeson, and soon a battle of wills begins, with twists that are best left for you to discover.

Speaking of Cushing, he’s barely in it, but he predictably makes the most of it with an understated performance that exudes a creepy yet strangely gentle quality; you wouldn’t want to be in the same room with this guy, especially if you’re a woman, but there’s something about him that suggests he’s not the person you should really be worried about. One scene of him standing before a noose while trying to unknot Geeson’s scarf brings to mind a bit in 1932’s White Zombie, while the visual symbolism concerning the violation of Geeson’s innocence becomes even more overt when Joan Collins arrives at the halfway point to kill a cute little bunny right in front of her.

It has a quiet, deliberate atmosphere, and everyone is excellent; Geeson in particular delivers an emotionally raw performance that can be uncomfortably real and difficult to watch. But I have to say that I don’t enjoy movies predicated on gaslighting the protagonist and dragging us along for the frustrating ride before things resolve; some may call it suspense, but as someone prone to anxiety, I call it cinematic torture.

I have quibbles with the final act, but no spoilers. Right from the precision-crafted opening sequence, you’ll see what you’re in for, perhaps more than you realize. And in addition to the moment that shockingly punctuates the end of that montage, the movie has one other arresting image that will stick with you involving Peter Cushing and his circular glasses; you’ll know when you see it.

As befits a box set that’s so clearly a labor-of-love tribute to this era of Hammer history, the extras are exhaustive and entertaining. The one criticism I have is that there are no captions on any of the extras, making them inaccessible for some fans. There’s no reason not to provide them, but Severin? Don’t ever generate them automatically; hire someone to write and edit them properly.

Since there are so many extras included on every film disc as well as an extra disc with Fear, let’s examine the 19 hours of material (!) by category:

There are two commentary tracks for each film. The first features Sangster from years back (he died in 2011), moderated by Hammer historian Marcus Hearn with actress Suzanna Leigh joining on Lust. Leigh brings out more energy in Sangster, although he’s informative and enjoyable in all of them. The second tracks feature various authors and experts pontificating about the production history and cultural impact of each film.

Besides the many newly produced interviews with cast and crew across all three films, there are archival segments featuring Cushing and Sangster. Many of them are relatively short, but they cover a wide range of perspectives, with some folks like production runner Philip Campbell talking about all three movies. Perhaps the most consistent mood is “wistful.” Kirsten Lindholm of Lust is a delightfully quirky highlight, and if (like me) you’re a Dracula A.D. 1972 fan, Christopher Neame’s interview serves as an overview of his entire career, including that film, his work in Lust, and the day Cushing told him the work was helping him to deal with his grief over his wife’s death.

That dedicated extras disc accompanying Fear includes three documentaries: one on Sangster (he’s credited with shaping the modern conception of Dracula and Frankenstein as well as demonstrating great versatility in multiple genres), one on Ralph Bates (it’s a heartfelt tribute from his wife, son, and colleagues), and one on Joan Collins (authors Kier-La Janisse and Amanda Reyes look at how the horror work Collins disowned led to her iconic turn in Dynasty).

Perhaps the most laudable aspect of this set is that with so much subject matter that should center a woman’s experience and perspective, they do just that, featuring an array of scholars and historians like Dr. Colin Azariah-Kribbs and Dr. Emma Liggins on the work of Mary Shelley; writer/producer Gillian Wallace Horvat and narrator Megan Stern on the history of Frankenstein adaptations; Carmen Maria Machado (she edited an edition of Carmilla) and Annie Rose Malamet on the cultural phenomenon of sapphic vampire tales; and two essays by Dr. Alexandra Heller-Nicholas on school-based stories and gaslighting as a thematic element of Fear.

If all this isn’t enough, there’s a 312-page full-color glossy volume titled Horror! Lust! Fear! Sangster — an overwhelming compilation of interviews and essays, rare photos, and even comic adaptations. The book offers a ton of information not touched on in the other extras, but in order to fit everything in the box, the book (otherwise designed beautifully by Stephen Thrower) is rather small and just a little awkward to read. It’s still a lovely, and one might argue indispensable, part of this once-in-a-lifetime set.

There’s plenty of additional bits and bobs too, like trailers and promos, alternate “clothed” takes, and TV opening credits. It’s a treasure trove, and if the material becomes repetitive, it’s still worth it to include everything Severin could collect.

articles.title: Ultra Graphics Settings Are a Scam: Why High Is Good Enough, if Not Better, for Most Players
articles.summary: Most games don’t actually need to be played at Ultra settings to look good. They don’t even need it to look great. To prove it, I turned down the settings in a bunch of great-looking games to see how much difference it really makes. Not only did I find it hard to spot any obvious visual difference in most of the games I tested, but performance went up dramatically and the smoother framerates were well worth the minimal sacrifice.
articles.body:
I’m a privileged gamer. As a hardware reviewer, over the years I’ve been sent top-tier CPUs and graphics cards , letting me bounce from one flagship to the next. That’s made me lazy at game settings. I often just set the game at whatever the maximum “Ultra” setting is and get on with playing. But by doing so, I’ve just been playing into the marketing hype – and leaving a lot of performance on the table, it turns out.

Most games don’t actually need to be played at Ultra settings to look good. They don’t even need it to look great. The latest upscaling technologies are fantastically good at emulating higher resolutions, and often the difference between Ultra and High settings isn’t something I even really notice if pushed to look.

As an experiment, I turned down the settings in a bunch of great-looking games to see how much difference it really makes. Not only did I find it hard to spot any obvious visual difference in most of the games I tested, but performance went up dramatically and the smoother framerates were well worth the minimal sacrifice.

I’ve been able to ignore graphics settings for so long due to a mix of low-demand game selection and high-end hardware. As I said, my current system is powerful, but I also mostly play older sim games and lighter indies.

With an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X3D and PowerColor Red Devil RX 7900 XTX, I have one of the fastest gaming CPUs on the market and the fastest graphics card AMD has ever made. It’s not quite an RTX 5080 or RTX 5090, so it’s not really designed with Ultra Path Tracing in mind, but it’s not a million miles away either. It’s more than capable of running almost any game at Ultra settings, at 4K, and sometimes even with ray tracing enabled.

That’s especially true once you throw in FSR upscaling and a little frame generation to smooth things out.

My plan for this test is to run a bunch of games at their very highest settings that are functionally playable – at least 30 FPS – with upscaling at Quality or native, without frame generation, and grab a few example screenshots of it in action. Then do so again at maxed out settings but with Balanced upscaling, and then a final test with everything turned down just one notch. So High, if Ultra is the top option, Medium if High is the best, etc.

Let’s jump in with what is arguably still one of the best looking games ever made, Cyberpunk 2077. If there’s one game that is guaranteed to bring my 7900XTX to its knees, it’s this one.

And yeah, Raytracing Overdrive Settings, 4K resolution, Path Tracing enabled, FSR set to Quality mode, it was a clunky slideshow mess. 20 FPS at best. But of course it looks incredible:

But you know what also looks incredible? Cyberpunk 2077 at those same settings with Balanced Upscaling. I just took these screenshots, and besides a few background details looking a little more lifelike and of-the-environment in the Quality screenshot, it’s very difficult to tell any difference.

Meanwhile, the performance difference meant it was actually playable.

Although Cyberpunk with ray tracing does look stunning, and its path tracing even more so in the right settings, I’d even argue switching it down to a mere Ultra settings without ray tracing looks almost as good.

It’s definitely more stylized than the real-time lighting effects of ray tracing, but CD Projekt Red did a fantastic job making Night City look real and alive, even with baked in lighting. I’d very happily play the whole game like this.

Alan Wake 2 is far from the glitz and ray-traced glamour of Night City, but it’s just as good looking in its own, dark, dirty way. It also eviscerated my system’s performance with everything absolutely turned up the nines. We’re talking 1-3 FPS. Unplayable. But gorgeous:

But it can very easily be both. Switching over to FSR Balanced, where it’s basically cutting the 4K resolution in half, the performance jumped up to perfectly playable for this type of more sedate game play. I genuinely can’t tell the difference, even when running around. It’s really impressive how far upscaling has come over the years.

I’d be tempted to leave it there, but there is additional performance to be had and not much in the way of a visual downgrade from trimming the fat even more. Switching everything to one notch down (High or Medium, depending on what the setting peaks at) and no ray tracing, gets you an almost-as-good-looking Alan Wake 2 experience.

Performance jumped enormously here, and this is where you want to play if you value smoother animation over pristine visuals. Especially since I still had to look close to spot the real differences. During actual game play, though? With a darker game like this where concealment and shadow is the game’s vibe, I don’t think many would notice.

How about a getting-older but a goodie? Hogwarts Legacy isn’t photo-realistic, but it is incredibly immersive. Making sure the game looks good is a huge part of the experience. Fortunately, you can get away with steering clear of ray tracing with this one. If you enable it, the experience is beautiful:

But I’d argue it’s just as beautiful with Balanced upscaling – notching an extra 15% fps for my trouble, and nudging over a more-comfortable 40 FPS.

Switching to more modest settings and dropping the RT entirely looks amazing too. This game doesn’t make enough use of the fancy-lighting technique to be worth it, I’d argue. Despite its prevalence in the graphics menu, this game looks phenomenal on more modest settings. Don’t fear dropping them down a notch or two.

Final Fantasy VII: Rebirth is not as pretty as the other games, but it’s one that uses an outsized quantity of VRAM. Fortunately, the 24GB on the 7900XTX had no trouble with it even pushed to the limit. But then, why would you bother?

Dropping to Balanced and cutting the rendering resolution by 40% didn’t appear to make much of a difference to how the game looked. There isn’t any more obvious aliasing on background elements, even the thinner pipes. Texture details remain.

Dropping everything to Medium/High setting depending does make more of an impact, but even then it’s something I had to actively look for, and when in motion it’s even less apparent.

It’s not nothing, but I don’t think it’s worth it

If your hardware supports it, playing games at their prettiest is lovely. It’s simple, it’s easy, and it looks great. Especially in static screenshots, or in the ideal circumstances. But so do games with heavier-handed upscaling, and even lowering the settings a little doesn’t strip them of their charm, or immersion. That also gives you extra performance and a smoother game, which I think is way more impactful than getting a few extra pixels, or slightly nicer lighting.

The point I’m trying to make with these comparisons isn’t that there’s no benefit to turning all the settings up to their maximum, but that the performance loss really isn’t worth it. Ultimately, it feels like those settings are a way to get better looking screenshots for the marketing campaign, and to give gamers something to aspire to. A dragon that we’ll forever be chasing, until the next game comes along.

Ultimately, if all you can game on is something lower than the maximum – which is almost all of us – then you really aren’t missing out on much.

Don’t look on in envy at the people spending $5,000 on a graphics card in 2026 . They’re getting a very-slightly-better looking gaming experience for the money. As prices continue to be ridiculous , I think lower settings are perfectly fine.

articles.title: Metal Gear Solid 4: The Flawed Masterpiece Kojima Didn't Want to Make
articles.summary: With Metal Gear Solid 4 finally arriving on modern consoles thanks to Master Collection Vol. 2, we take a look back at the game's legacy. Was it really just a big cutscene, or is it Kojima's masterpiece?
articles.body:
This is an IGN opinion piece from Charlie Lopresto, who believes that love can bloom, even on a battlefield. He first encountered Metal Gear Solid on a demo disc from Pizza Hut and has since completed three hundred missions in VR– the kind that’s indistinguishable from the real thing.

Like Old Snake, Metal Gear Solid 4: Guns of the Patriots is a fossil. A genetic dead-end of gaming evolution, the unhinged and overflowing masterpiece that barely left a mark on the artform. Despite its commercial and critical success , MGS4 is rarely regarded as top tier Metal Gear. But is that actually fair?

Trapped on dead console hardware for the better part of its hard life, thanks to the new Master Collection Vol. 2 it’s finally possible for everyone to experience MGS4, from series diehards who first fired it up in 2008 to people completely new to Metal Gear who have absolutely no idea what they’re in for.

All of them will reckon with the many, many questions MGS4 brings to mind, like: Will we ever see a game like this again? Why did we stop talking about it? And, perhaps most importantly: MGS4 is really good, isn't it?

Hideo Kojima did not want to make Metal Gear Solid 4. He publicly declared his desire to end the franchise as early as MGS 2, then proclaimed that he was finished with the saga after Snake Eater. Kojima’s words were weary but his deeds said otherwise. He wasn’t really ready to move on– both of those games ooze with a sense of momentum and life.

Guns of the Patriots feels different. There’s a gloomy weight to the game, like a funeral – the raucous kind where friends, grudges, and flames gather to settle scores, awkwardly hook up, and celebrate the end.

Prior to MGS4, we’d last seen Solid Snake in 2001, when he dropped a prophetic monologue and vanished into the streets of lower Manhattan shortly after the former President of the United States crashed into the city with a giant sci-fi submarine. As situations go, it’s certainly one that begs for some followup, and after years of fans demanding the return of the Legendary Mercenary, Kojima obliged in trademark trolling fashion.

You don’t get the cocky, mech-smashing super soldier who slays Tengu by the dozen with a metafictional bandana. Kojima, who reportedly received death threats over his reluctance to move the story forward with MGS4, instead delivers a feeble, actively decomposing relic. Old Snake grunts, screams, coughs and gags wetly as he crawls in agony through his final mission, all for the privilege of being allowed to die before his poisoned blood wipes out humanity. Old Snake was punished before Punished was cool.

It’s a trope we’ve seen a lot lately: the beloved hero of a bygone age, bitter, broken down, and humbled, all in service of passing the torch to a spunky new recruit before the credits roll. But there is no Rey to don the cardboard box here, no Adonis Creed, no Robin, nor any kind of chipper next-gen protagonist queued to continue Snake’s legacy by selling some video games. Nearly everyone in Metal Gear Solid 4 is old, dead, or extremely married by the end of the story, a bittersweet and beautifully conclusive eulogy to a deeply heroic and thoroughly decrepit old man who reeks of cigarettes.

Modern media is designed to protect itself, to keep mythology marketable and leave endings open for future exploitation. Kojima does the exact opposite with MGS4, performing peaceful euthanasia on his life’s work to that point. It’s a brave move delivered with a lot of love and earnestness, and anyone upset at geriatric Snake were too busy feasting on a buffet of fanservice to stay mad for long.

Rarely do sprawling stories wrap up as neatly as Metal Gear Solid’s, even if “neatly” here means bursting at the seams and slightly slapdash. Kojima didn’t have a decades-long master plan when he made Metal Gear for the MSX in 1987, but managed to B.S. his way into satisfying answers for nearly everything. It’s an ambitious, messy, and sincere sendoff to Snake and the series. There’s really nowhere else to go from here.

Which brings us to the elephant in the room, dangling precariously from a Fulton balloon over this discussion: Guns of the Patriots is not the last Metal Gear Solid game. Despite his protestations, Kojima had two more Metal Gears in him: the portable Peace Walker, a numbered entry in all but name, and the tragic MGS5. Both respect the brick wall he built at the end of the timeline and tread water safely in the past instead of pushing forward. Kojima decided to move the series horizontally instead, experimenting with tech and form until Konami kicked him out.

Kojima’s actual final chapter, when it came, was compromised and ignominious, a casualty of his ugly exit from Konami and a sour note on which to end. Guns of the Patriots was Kojima ending things on his own terms; a bombastic epic with a massive budget that bursts with supreme confidence and unfiltered honesty. It would be the last time he ever made a game like this.

Guns of the Patriots, like every mainline Metal Gear game before it, is structured like a linear, cinematic action-adventure story. It’s almost quaint from a 2026 lens, when half the industry runs on open worlds and the other on live-service menuslop, but this was Kojima’s M.O. throughout the early part of his career.

And yet for something so committed to telling one continuous story in agonizing detail, MGS4 feels oddly episodic. Each of its five acts is practically a different genre. One minute you’re scooching across a battlefield, then next you’re skulking through the streets of Eastern Europe in a trenchcoat. Kojima drops us into warzones and weapons facilities across the globe, introduces new ideas, and moves past them just as quickly.

A much-hyped faction loyalty system stops mattering after Act 2, and the mechanic to manipulate enemy emotions isn’t really a factor until New Game Plus. There are a whopping 70 guns available for Snake that are largely superfluous, while the omnipresent Psyche meter quickly fades into the background outside of some perfectly-timed comedy. It’s like Kojima is cramming every single cockamamie “Metal Gear” idea he had left into the game as if it were his last chance, or so he hoped.

Kojima’s Hollywood aspirations run wild here, and while some of the sloggier cinematics are a chore, I’d sit through a thousand torturous mission briefings to relive MGS4’s queasy, white-knuckle fusions of story and mechanics, like the sicko mode split screen action setpieces and the tactile desperation of the microwave hallway.

The game’s linearity is a huge strength. We embody Old Snake through every second of his grueling ordeal. We wince with every injury and every brutal negging. Solid Snake was our stand-in from the moment he infiltrated Outer Heaven, detours aside, and we feel every moment of the long journey as he slugs it out with “Liquid” one last time. That sense of embodiment, being inside Snake, a part of him… you can’t get that from a mission select screen. But Kojima’s next and last games in his Metal Gear Solid saga would be built with these impersonal menus in mind.

Frustrated with the PS3’s limitations for his grand scale vision, Kojima went small instead. Also available in Master Collection Vol. 2, Metal Gear Solid: Peace Walker was originally built for the handheld Playstation Portable, so a sprawling linear opus was pretty much off the table without the luxury of blu-ray discs and Cell processors. Instead, he designed for the handheld system’s strengths: short, snackable stealth missions selected from a menu, perfect for a train ride or waiting room.

Previous Metal Gears relied on blockbuster storytelling to keep you coming back, but Peace Walker leans on moreish base-building, optional challenges, and RPG systems borrowed from Monster Hunter to keep you hooked. Seven years after Snake bluntslid across the Big Shell, grinding was back in Metal Gear, and this time it was here to stay.

Kojima is clearly fond of the results. He considers Peace Walker the fifth mainline MGS game, and thanks to rereleases it’s had far more staying power than the average PSP game. He liked the formula so much that he made it his default going forward: both MGS5 and the Death Stranding games run on the same skeleton, embracing timers and stats and judging your performance in isolated missions chosen from a list. At this rate we’ll probably be chasing S-ranks in OD.

It works beautifully for a handheld, and for a taciturn cipher like Sam Bridges, but it really doesn’t suit traditional Metal Gear Solid. MGS5 was free from the shackles of a 272p screen, but even with the full glory of the Fox Engine, the menu-driven mode of interaction keeps us at arms length from Snake.

The story becomes another checklist item, grinding through side ops until an actually important mission appears on the list. We’re watching from a more omniscient remove as Snake sizes up the stats of future subordinates and navigates a tech tree. For a series that loves to mess directly with the player and collapse the space between them and the character, losing that intimacy comes with a cost. MGS4 made Snake’s suffering feel like ours, and the series never approached that level of pathos again.

Being inside Old Snake’s head for dozens of hours is genuinely unpleasant at times, to the point it makes the game almost hard to revisit, and it’s one of several reasons why MGS4’s legacy is so quiet.

It’s hard for a game to have an ongoing influence when nobody can play it. Metal Gear Solid 4 has been unavailable for years, buried alive on hardware that Sony hasn’t sold for nearly a decade. Countless classic titles are trapped on ancient tech, but it’s rare for a numbered entry in a massive, triple A series.

The PS3’s Cell Processor was notoriously miserable to develop for, with bizarre architecture far removed from industry standards that made porting anything off it a nightmare. It’s also why emulation, so vital to keeping commercially abandoned games alive, couldn’t save Old Snake either. Strides have been made recently, but MGS4 remains a genuine bear to run outside of its native hardware.

None of these technical woes were insurmountable, and neither were the super specific Sony references or the licensing entanglements from MGS4’s frankly ludicrous product placement. It just needed a publisher that cared enough to devote the resources to porting it and had the courage to get Uniqlo, Apple, and Playboy back to the negotiating table.

Konami was content to let the series languish for a long time as it explicitly abandoned video games for pachinko parlors. It only once really wrestled with following MGS4 in the timeline, in Platinum’s audacious spinoff Metal Gear Rising: Revengeance . Otherwise, it didn’t matter to Konami if nobody could buy or play MGS4.

Thankfully, that’s changed. Konami’s prodigal return to video games has gone well enough so far, and now MGS4 is enjoying an immaculate rebirth, iPod and all. How will modern gamers receive it after so many years in the wilderness?

Guns of the Patriots is an aggressively unfriendly game by modern standards, and the cutscenes are completely out of control. A common Kojima criticism is that he’d rather make movies than games, but it’s hard to think of any film that’s nine hours long, built largely out of static codec calls, and features extended scenes of people drinking soda and smoking around little girls while weeping about nanomachines and infectious diseases. Whatever MGS4 is, it’s not a movie, and it’s certainly not made for newcomers.

MGS4 isn’t spoken of in the same breath as the first three games, and when it does come up it’s rarely for what it actually accomplished. And since almost nobody’s been able to play the game for so long, its reputation as an uncomfortable cutscene parade is all that remains. Opinion calcifies when there’s nothing around to contradict it.

That’s not to say nobody’s tried to pick up what MGS4 put down. Resident Evil Requiem almost feels like a tribute at times, a last ride for a long-suffering hero who makes a pilgrimage back to where his story started while dying from a sci-fi disease that makes him cough a lot. By the end, Leon is upgrading his weapons with counterfeit Drebin Points, dueling hand-to-hand with his longtime rival, and dragging himself inch by agonizing inch through a high-tech hallway.

Without spoiling where it lands, Requiem doesn’t have the nerve to go out on a limb like MGS4. Its tribute to Raccoon City sent us on a nostalgic trip through a place we’ve already walked through twice in HD, stopping far short of the wobbly PSX vertices in MGS4’s homage to Shadow Moses, another holy gaming space introduced in 1998. The ending stops short as well, a clean cut affair that leaves plenty of room for further adventures and profitable sequels.

Triple-A gaming didn’t go in an MGS4 direction in the intervening years. Budgets are too big and bosses too demanding to allow a freakazoid like Kojima off the leash again– unless you’re the man himself, of course. But Kojima only gets away with that because he had the power to leave the system that made MGS4 possible. Everyone else is still answering to a spreadsheet and, understandably, gunshy about unfettered visionaries.

Modern gaming’s play-it-safe instincts could do wonders for MGS4’s reputation. George Lucas and his Star Wars prequels suffered a similar rap over the years, dismissed as the bloated self-indulgent work of an auteur no one could rein in. But a decade of focus-tested corpo Star Wars sequels has sparked a genuine re-evaluation of the much-maligned Episodes I, 2, and 3, and now that it’s available again, MGS4 deserves the same treatment. Both the prequels and MGS4 are messy, overstuffed, and often embarrassing, but they are never once indifferent. Sincerity ages a lot better than caution.

Ultimately, everyone has to judge Metal Gear Solid 4 for themselves, to witness the grandiosity, endure the hour-plus uninterrupted cutscenes, and gaze hypnotically at Old Snake’s buttcheeks amidst a bombardment of jargon and lore. At least now you’ll get the chance to, and when you do finally sit with Kojima’s wayward masterpiece, you might like it more than you’d think.

Charlie "Moose" Lopresto graduated law school, passed the bar, and made a financially questionable decision to write about games and movies instead. Contributing to IGN since 2021, he collects solo board games and transforming robots.
